## Two investors, one question. Who is told to hold more stock? {#hook}

::: {.split .narrow .center-v}
::: {.prose}
Emily lives in Ohio and Yuki in Osaka. Both are 40, both have the local equivalent of \$50,000 to invest, and both have a standard pension.

Each asks a chatbot how much to put into a stock index fund.

[The share of U.S. adults who use AI tools for financial advice roughly doubled between 2024 and 2025 (Financial Health Network 2025). A handful of models answer them, in every language.]{.note}
:::

```{=html}
<div class="stage" data-chart="hook"></div>
```
:::

::: {.notes}
The hook. Emily and Yuki are the running example for the whole talk. They are fictional, and every number attached to them is the United States or the Japan cell of the real collection.

Read the question out. Then the bet: "Show of hands. Who thinks Yuki is told to hold less stock than Emily? More? About the same?" Most rooms say less. If they hesitate, give them the textbook reason: a yen investor who buys a world index fund carries exchange-rate risk that a dollar investor does not, so a careful advisor might give Yuki less. That reason comes back on the benchmark slide.

Hold the silence for a second, then advance.
:::

## Where you live moves the advice 12 points. Which model you ask moves it 34. {#reveal}

::: {.split .narrow .center-v}
::: {.prose}
Yuki is told to hold as much stock as Emily: [ ]{.data key="c.Japan.mean" pct="0"}% against [ ]{.data key="c.USA.mean" pct="0"}%, averaged over 650 answers each.

Across the 21 countries the averages span [ ]{.data key="stats.meanMin" pct="0"} to [ ]{.data key="stats.meanMax" pct="0"}%. Across the 13 models they span [ ]{.data key="stats.modelMin" pct="0"} to [ ]{.data key="stats.modelMax" pct="0"}%, or \$17,000 of the \$50,000.

::: {.stats .two}
::: {.stat}
[[ ]{.data key="variance.q1.model" d="0"}%]{.k .f}
[of the variance in the answers comes from which model is asked]{.l}
:::
::: {.stat}
[[ ]{.data key="variance.q1.country" d="0"}%]{.k .f}
[from which country, the rest from their interaction and repetition]{.l}
:::
:::

[[The model grid](#room-models) · [Why 60?](#room-round) · [Eleven weeks later](#room-tracking)]{.rooms}
:::

```{=html}
<div class="stage" data-chart="reveal" data-animate="once"></div>
```
:::

::: {.notes}
The payoff. The stage builds in: the 21 country averages drop in and huddle, then the 13 model averages spread out from the middle. Let it finish, about five seconds, before speaking.

Say: Emily and Yuki get the same answer. The whole spread across countries is twelve points. Across models it is thirty-four, which is $17,000 of the $50,000. In the ranges that is three times as much. In a variance decomposition it is twelve times: model identity 70 percent, the country 6.

If the animation does not run, the finished picture is already there.

Questions: "which models?" opens the grid room. "Why 60?" opens the round-numbers room: every answer is a multiple of five. "Is this just July's models?" opens the September room: the model still dominates, though less so among the newest models.
:::

## Prior work varies the investor and holds the country fixed {#literature}

::: {.claims}
- **Choukhmane, de Silva, Lin and Akuzawa (2026).** U.S. households' own prompts, set against a calibrated life-cycle model. The advice is moderately risk averse and leans on round numbers.
- **Ross and Lo (2026).** A thousand synthetic U.S. clients and one vendor's models. Stated risk tolerance carries most of the weight, which they call heuristic collapse.
- **Foltyn and Olsson (2026).** The design this paper adapts, with the investor's gender as the treatment. The gaps are under two percentage points.
- **This paper.** The country and its language as the treatment, 21 countries and 13 models, a country-calibrated benchmark, and the explanation text kept and coded.
:::

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds. The first two are the closest papers, and both hold the investor's country fixed by construction. Ross and Lo reach the same conclusion about the advice rule from the other direction, which strengthens both readings.

Foltyn and Olsson is the framework this experiment adapts, replacing gender with country. Keep their under-two-points gender gap in mind as a yardstick.

For robo-advice people: D'Acunto, Prabhala and Rossi (2019) and Rossi and Utkus (2024) find first-generation robo-advisors improving diversification. LLMs differ in being general-purpose and deployed in every language at once. Human advisors already give one-size-fits-all advice (Foerster et al. 2017).
:::

## Three versions of each prompt separate the language from the country and its institutions {#design}

```{=html}
<div class="three">
  <div class="vcard">
    <div class="vtag">Version B</div>
    <div class="vsub">Japanese · country named · generic instruments</div>
    <div class="chat ask yuki jp">…それ以外に<span class="cue">標準的な年金プラン</span>に加入しています。<span class="cue">現在は日本に住んでいます。</span>…幅広い株式市場をカバーするインデックスファンドと国債…<span class="gloss">a standard pension plan · I live in Japan · a broad stock index fund and government bonds</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="vcard">
    <div class="vtag">Version B-cross</div>
    <div class="vsub">English · country named · generic instruments</div>
    <div class="chat ask yuki">…I have <span class="cue">a standard pension plan</span> otherwise. <span class="cue">I live in Japan.</span> I am thinking of splitting my investment between a broad stock market index fund and some government bonds…<span class="gloss">the same yen amount, ¥7,500,000</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="vcard">
    <div class="vtag">Version C</div>
    <div class="vsub">Japanese · country named · local instruments</div>
    <div class="chat ask yuki jp">…<span class="cue">通常のiDeCo口座があり、国民年金に加入しています</span>。私は日本に住んでいます。…<span class="cue">eMAXIS Slim All Country</span>…<span class="cue">日本国債（JGB）</span>…<span class="gloss">an iDeCo account and the national pension · eMAXIS Slim All Country · JGBs</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="contrasts">
  <span>B across 21 countries <em>the country and its language together</em></span>
  <span>B against B-cross <em>the language alone</em></span>
  <span>C against B <em>the local instruments alone</em></span>
</div>
<div class="strip">
  <span><b>267,150</b>answers</span><span><b>13</b>models from 6 vendors</span><span><b>21</b>countries</span><span><b>50</b>answers per cell</span><span><b>2 July 2026</b>pre-registered, collected 3–4 July</span>
</div>
<p class="strip-note">Also varied: the investor's age (30, 40, 55) and two further questions, on a mortgage and on inflation.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
The design in one slide. Fifteen countries are asked in the local language and six in English (U.S., UK, Canada, Australia, India, South Africa), so B-cross exists for the fifteen. The amount is the round local-currency equivalent of $50,000 in native number format.

The same prompt returns different answers each time at temperature 0.7, which is why every cell is asked 50 times. The instructions block with the JSON schema is English everywhere. Only the question is translated, by DeepL, then reviewed by native speakers in all fifteen languages.

"Where is Version A?" A translated prompt that named no country. It was dropped before collection because it could not separate the language from the style of a translation. The letters follow the pre-registration.

Primary cell for everything that follows: the portfolio question, Version B, age 40.
:::

## The seven countries that differ from the U.S. are all told to hold less stock {#countries}

::: {.split .narrow .center-v}
::: {.prose}
Seven of twenty contrasts survive the Holm correction for testing twenty countries at once, from Mexico at [ ]{.data key="c.Mexico.fe.est" d="1"} to Brazil at [ ]{.data key="c.Brazil.fe.est" d="1"} points.

Brazil's gap moves \$5,500 of the \$50,000 into bonds. That is a third of the model spread, and it is not zero.

Yuki's Japan sits at [ ]{.data key="c.Japan.fe.est" d="1" sign=""} points, with an interval from [ ]{.data key="c.Japan.fe.lo" d="1"} to [ ]{.data key="c.Japan.fe.hi" d="1" sign=""}.

[Joint test of equal advice in all 21 countries: p = 0.006, wild cluster bootstrap over the 13 models.]{.source}

[[How the inference works](#room-inference) · [Robustness](#room-robust)]{.rooms}
:::

```{=html}
<div class="stage" data-chart="countries"></div>
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Point at the top: Brazil, Italy, Poland, France, Spain, the Netherlands, Mexico. Southern and central Europe plus Latin America. Every contrast that survives is negative, and the U.S. sits near the top of the band.

The yardstick for the rest of the talk: country effects are 3 to 11 points. That is small beside the 34-point model spread and beside what the stated investor does later, but larger than the under-two-points gender gaps of Foltyn and Olsson.

Whether these gaps are errors is the benchmark slide's question. Brazil's benchmark is low, so its gap may be a move toward theory.

Inference: model fixed effects and clustering by model. With 13 clusters every p-value is a wild cluster bootstrap with Webb weights. The minimum detectable single contrast is about four points, so the nulls rule out large gaps, not gaps of a point or two. If asked about the rank of the covariance matrix: the joint test is the bootstrap Wald statistic. The asymptotic cluster-robust test can impose only 12 of the 20 restrictions with 13 clusters, and it also rejects, F(12, 12) = 34.26.
:::

## Language and local instruments move the advice about a point, so the country reference carries the rest {#language}

::: {.stats .two}
::: {.stat}
[[ ]{.data key="stats.lambda" d="1"}]{.k .f}
[points when the question is asked in the local language instead of English, same country and amount (B against B-cross, 15 countries, p = [ ]{.data key="stats.lambdaP" d="3"})]{.l}
:::
::: {.stat}
[[ ]{.data key="stats.phi" d="1"}]{.k .f}
[points when the prompt names the local pension, government bonds and index fund (C against B, 20 countries, p = [ ]{.data key="stats.phiP" d="3"})]{.l}
:::
:::

::: {.prose}
What remains of each country's gap attaches to the country reference itself, which in these prompts also changes the currency and the amount.

[Pre-registered tests of the language and local-context effects, the portfolio question at age 40, model and country fixed effects.]{.source}

[[Country-by-country decomposition](#room-decomp) · [The dollar-denominated stake](#room-robust)]{.rooms}
:::

::: {.notes}
Two numbers, each about a point. Asking Yuki's question in Japanese rather than English lowers the share by 1.3 points: significant, and an order of magnitude below the largest country effects. Naming iDeCo, eMAXIS Slim and JGBs moves it by −0.7, not significant at 5 percent.

Why a small language effect is plausible: interpretability work finds that multilingual models solve tasks in a shared concept space that sits closer to English than to any other language (Wendler et al. 2024). It was not guaranteed: the same model often asserts different facts in different languages.

The United Kingdom is the pre-registered test of naming a country without changing the language: +0.7 points, interval −0.8 to +2.2, inside the ±5 margin registered for that test alone.

The country reference also changes the currency and the numeral. The dollar-stake cell rules the numeral out for Germany, Japan and Sweden.

Bridge: so the name of the country moves the number a little. Does the model know anything about the country?
:::

Yuki's answer also cites the 100-minus-age rule, in Japanese, and Emily's calls 60/40 classic. The number is the same retail convention in both languages.

## The explanations localize, and the number barely moves {#words}

::: {.split .narrow .center-v}
::: {.prose}
A separate model, shown only the explanation text, codes whether it names local instruments, taxes or pensions.

It finds local context in [ ]{.data key="c.USA.localB" pct="0"}% of U.S. answers and in [ ]{.data key="stats.localMinNonUS" pct="0"} to [ ]{.data key="stats.localMaxNonUS" pct="0"}% elsewhere.

[ ]{.live-note}

[Pre-registered text tests, Version B and C, age 40.]{.source}

[[How the text is coded](#room-coding)]{.rooms}
:::

```{=html}
<div class="stage tall" data-chart="words"></div>
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Start on Version B. Point at the two coloured rows: the U.S. at 18 percent and Japan at 54. Outside the U.S. the models reach for local instruments, taxes and pensions in half to nearly all of their explanations. So they know where the investor lives. Both panels share one 0 to 100 percent scale: the words range across the whole axis, the numbers sit in a narrow band.

The move: flip the switch to Version C, where the prompt names each country's own pension, bonds and index fund. The hatched bars jump toward 100 percent, a 23-point rise, and the dots barely move, −0.7 points pooled. Dashed rings mark where each dot was. Brazil moves most, about 3 points, and the pooled effect is not significant at 5 percent.

The same country regression that finds a few points on the equity share finds up to 78 points on whether local context is named, so the design can see country variation where the answers contain it.

Objection, "the coder just finds the words you put in the prompt": that is why Version B, which names no instruments, is the main test, and 47 to 96 percent there is unprompted. Under Version C the U.S. rate rises from 18 to 84 percent, so the coder does count U.S. instruments as local context.

If the switch fails, the caption carries the result.
:::

## On the mortgage question, the country matters more than the model {#mortgage}

::: {.split .wide-left .center-v}
```{=html}
<div class="stage tall" data-chart="three"></div>
```

::: {.prose}
Same models, same design, a different question: should Yuki invest spare savings or use them to prepay a 4% mortgage?

A third question asks how to protect savings that earn 1% against 3% inflation.

[ ]{.live-note}

[On inflation, the answer in Brazil, Turkey and Mexico switches to inflation-linked bonds.]{.note}

[[Mortgage benchmark](#room-mortbench) · [Inflation instruments](#room-inflation)]{.rooms}
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Start on Portfolio: the picture from before, everything within a few points of the U.S. line, and the variance panel at model 70, country 6.

The move: click Mortgage. Fifteen countries slide 10 to 29 points to the left, Japan furthest, then China, Switzerland and Germany: the low-inflation economies, where a fixed nominal 4 percent is a high real rate. Yuki is told to invest 54 percent of her savings, Emily 82. The diamonds are the five countries where 4 percent is far below local rates, and there the advice stays near the U.S. level. The variance panel flips: the model's share falls to 15 percent and the country's rises to 27. The rest, 58 percent, is the model-by-country interaction and repetition noise.

Then click Inflation: Japan is again furthest from the U.S., at −11. On that question the choice of instrument localizes too: 87 percent of Brazilian answers recommend inflation-linked bonds, against 3 percent in the U.S.

Objection, "4 percent is above Japanese market rates, so prepaying just means escaping a bad loan": that strengthens the case for prepaying, and the benchmark room takes the contract rate as given. There, advice sits 13 to 36 points above the benchmark in every calibration country, so the localization is in the ordering more than in the level.
:::

## The uniform advice fails to calibrate across countries only if currency risk should count {#bench}

::: {.split .narrow .center-v}
::: {.prose}
Theory for the stake alone is the Merton share $(\mu - r)/(\gamma \sigma_c^{2})$, with the fund read as a world index and $\sigma_c$ its volatility in the investor's currency.

[ ]{.live-note}

[Counting pension and human capital as safe wealth, theory says 100% everywhere. Does a stated balance sheet move the advice?]{.bridge}

[[National preferences and literacy](#room-prefs) · [The benchmark](#room-benchmark)]{.rooms}
:::

```{=html}
<div class="stage tall" data-chart="bench"></div>
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Start unhedged. Teal rings are what theory prescribes, vermilion dots what the models say. Theory spreads over thirty-two points, from 21 percent in Turkey to 53 in Korea. The advice spans twelve, and a regression of advice on theory gives a slope of 0.13, which rejects one and does not reject zero. The slope rests on Brazil and Turkey.

The move: switch on the hedge. Every ring slides onto 52 percent, and the advice sits within six points of it in every country. This is true by construction, since the equity premium is common by uncovered interest parity and only the volatility differs, and that is the point: the whole spread in theory was exchange-rate risk.

What to say: under integrated markets the risky portfolio is the same world index everywhere, which rationalizes uniform advice. So the uniformity is defensible. The balance sheet is where theory and the advice part: counting pensions and human capital, theory is at the 100 percent corner in every country.

The bet for the next slide, while this one is still up: "Emily adds one sentence to her prompt. Which moves her recommendation more: saying she is investing for twenty years rather than one, or saying she will receive a generous pension?" Theory says the pension. Take the hands, then advance.
:::

## A stated horizon moves the advice 40 points. A stated pension moves it by one. {#levers}

::: {.stack}
::: {.prose}
One sentence about the investor, added to the English prompt in all 21 countries. A one-year horizon gets [ ]{.data key="stated.cells.h1" pct="0"}% in stocks and a twenty-year horizon [ ]{.data key="stated.cells.h20" pct="0"}%. [[The exact sentences](#room-wording)]{.rooms}
:::

```{=html}
<div class="stage tall" data-chart="levers" data-animate="once"></div>
```
:::

::: {.notes}
The payoff for the bet on the previous slide. The bars grow in one by one. Say the numbers as they land. Stated risk tolerance: +46 points, from 30 to 78 percent. Horizon, twenty years against one: +40. Generous pension: −1.0 for the risk-averse investor, +2.6 for the risk-tolerant one. For scale, the largest country contrast is Brazil at −11, and language and instruments are about a point.

The teal marks are theory's direction only. With constant relative risk aversion and independent returns the horizon is irrelevant. A lifecycle planner who counts pension wealth treats a generous pension as a bond and holds more stock.

Why English: the statements are added to the English prompt (Version B in the six English-speaking countries, B-cross elsewhere), so no translation stands between the sentence and the model.

Objection, "a one-year horizon is a spending date, and any planner holds bonds for that": the twenty-year cell alone sits about 20 points above the five-year prompt with no added sentence, so the response is not only year-one liquidity.

Ross and Lo find the same dominance of risk tolerance with one vendor. New here: 13 models, 21 countries, and the contrast with a stated pension.
:::

## The pattern fits a retail risk questionnaire, not a portfolio planner {#lineup}

```{=html}
<table class="lineup">
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th>A stated…</th>
      <th>Merton planner<span class="sub">the stake alone, CRRA, i.i.d. returns</span></th>
      <th>Lifecycle planner<span class="sub">the stake inside the whole balance sheet</span></th>
      <th class="col-win">Retail risk questionnaire<span class="sub">how do you feel about losses, when do you need the money</span></th>
      <th>Measured</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td class="cue-name">risk tolerance</td><td class="pred">raises it</td><td class="pred">raises it</td><td class="pred col-win">raises it</td><td class="meas"><span class="data" data-key="stated.risk.est" data-d="0" data-sign=""></span></td></tr>
    <tr><td class="cue-name">20-year horizon</td><td class="pred miss">no effect</td><td class="pred miss">no effect</td><td class="pred col-win">raises it</td><td class="meas"><span class="data" data-key="stated.horizon.est" data-d="0" data-sign=""></span></td></tr>
    <tr><td class="cue-name">generous pension</td><td class="pred">no effect</td><td class="pred miss">raises it a lot</td><td class="pred col-win blank">no effect, it is not asked</td><td class="meas"><span class="data" data-key="stated.pension.est" data-d="0"></span></td></tr>
    <tr class="verdict"><td></td><td>Contradicted on the horizon</td><td>Contradicted on the horizon and the pension</td><td class="win col-win">Consistent with all three</td><td></td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
```

::: {.prose}
[Measured: the stated-investor effects of the previous slide, in percentage points. Struck through and marked ✗: a prediction the measured effect contradicts. The comparison follows the popular-advice reading of Canner, Mankiw and Weil (1997) and Choi (2022).]{.source}
:::

::: {.notes}
Walk the columns left to right. The Merton planner gets risk tolerance and the pension right, because on the stake alone a pension does not enter, but it predicts no horizon effect, and the data show forty points. The lifecycle planner is contradicted twice. The questionnaire asks the two questions the models respond to and does not ask about the balance sheet.

The questionnaire column is the one reading consistent with all three. It is a reading, and the paper says "fits", not "proves". The levels also fit a Merton planner with relative risk aversion between 2 and 5, so the levels alone cannot discriminate. The comparative statics can.

Objection, "mean reversion rationalizes the horizon effect" (Campbell and Viceira 2002): yes, but a planner sophisticated enough to price return dynamics into forty points should not ignore pension wealth.

Bridge: the pension null is not blindness, though. The next slide shows the balance sheet does register, on one side.
:::

## Stated risks cut the stock share sharply, stated safety barely raises it {#asym}

::: {.split .narrow .center-v}
::: {.prose}
Three pairs of sentences, each adding exposure or safety to the investor's balance sheet.

A pension in stocks and a stake that is all of the investor's liquid wealth cut the share by [ ]{.data key="probes.0.r.est" d="1" abs=""} and [ ]{.data key="probes.1.r.est" d="1" abs=""} points. Their mirror statements raise it by [ ]{.data key="probes.0.s.est" d="1"} and [ ]{.data key="probes.1.s.est" d="1"}.

A currency hedge, the direct test of the benchmark slide, moves nothing.

[Exploratory probes collected in August 2026, after the pre-registered results were examined.]{.source}
:::

```{=html}
<div class="stage tall" data-chart="asym"></div>
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Read the pairs top to bottom. A pension invested in stocks: −17 points, the right sign. A guaranteed inflation-linked annuity, which should crowd stock in: +4.8, barely significant. The stake is all my liquid wealth: −23. The stake is a third of my liquid wealth with twice as much in safe savings: +2.5, when the benchmark is already at its 100 percent corner. The hedge: nothing either way, for a statement that should matter most where currencies are volatile.

What to say: the models de-risk on stated exposure and let stated safety raise the share very little. The paper calls this one-sided prudence rather than blindness. The neglected side is the margin that suitability rules oblige a human advisor to weigh.

Objection, "all my liquid wealth means no emergency buffer, and cutting stock is standard advice": agreed, and the benchmark has the same sign. The asymmetry is on the safe side, where a large cushion barely moves the number.

The wealth statements were asked in the U.S. prompt only. Everything here is exploratory and post hoc, tested two-sided against the benchmark's sign.
:::

## The portfolio answer follows the model and a questionnaire far more than the country {#conclusion}

::: {.claims}
- **Small, one-sided country effects.** Country averages span 12 points, model averages 34. The seven significant contrasts are all negative, 3 to 11 points. With a hedged world fund, theory prescribes 52% everywhere.
- **Local words, a nearly unchanged number.** Local context appears in 47 to 96% of non-U.S. explanations. Naming the local instruments raises that by 23 points and moves the share by −0.7.
- **Localization where local prices decide.** On the mortgage question the country explains 27% of the variance and the model 15%.
- **A questionnaire, not a balance-sheet rule.** Stated tolerance moves the advice 46 points and horizon 40, a stated pension about 1. Stated risks cut the share by up to 23 points, stated safety raises it by at most 5.
:::

::: {.prose}
[Each of a handful of models answers households in every language, so an error in its rule reaches everyone who asks it.]{.q}
:::

::: {.notes}
Four claims, one breath each. Then the market-structure sentence: advice used to be a nationally segmented service, walled in by regulation, trust and language. The same handful of models now answer in every language at negligible marginal cost, outside the regulatory perimeter that bound human advisors. The error is common within a model, across all the households that ask it.

Limits, if asked: no model internals, so the shared-representation reading is an inference from behaviour. The benchmark is static and closed form. The panel moves fast, though the September re-collection keeps the structure.
:::

## Which model is asked matters more than any country {#room-models visibility="uncounted"}

```{=html}
<div class="stage tall" data-chart="grid"></div>
```

[[Back to the talk](#reveal)]{.figcap}

::: {.notes}
Each cell is 50 answers. Read a column: a model gives nearly the same number to every country. Read a row: a country gets whatever its model gives. The model ordering follows neither vendor nor scale: Google's models span nearly the whole range, and the four Anthropic models all sit above the pooled mean.

Variance shares on the primary cell: model 69.5 percent, country 5.7, their interaction 9.5, repetitions 15.3. Equal-weighted over this panel, not market-share weighted.
:::

## Every answer is a round number, and 60 is the mode at age 40 {#room-round visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.stack}
::: {.prose}
Every one of 13,639 answers in the primary cell is a multiple of five, 85% are multiples of ten, and none is below 10 or above 80. Advice falls [ ]{.data key="slopes.pooled" d="2" abs=""} points per year of age against the rule's 1.00, and just as steeply where pensions are generous.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="stage" data-chart="round"></div>
```
:::

[[Back to the talk](#reveal)]{.figcap}

::: {.notes}
Age 30 is told 6.2 points more than age 40 and age 55 11.1 points less. The interaction with the pension replacement rate is an exact zero (ψ = −0.0002, p = 0.96): the same glide path in the most and least generous pension systems.

The deviations from the rule go toward conservatism at both ends, where Love (2013) puts the optimum above the rule. This is the same early-life conservatism Choukhmane et al. (2026) find a life-cycle model cannot rationalize. Exploratory, not pre-registered.
:::

## Eleven weeks later, the model still explains far more of the advice than the country {#room-tracking visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.stats}
::: {.stat}
[[ ]{.data key="tracking.2026-07-04.model" d="0"}% · [ ]{.data key="tracking.2026-07-04.country" d="0"}%]{.k .f}
[model and country shares of the variance, July collection, one English prompt per country, 13 models]{.l}
:::
::: {.stat}
[[ ]{.data key="tracking.2026-09-19.model" d="0"}% · [ ]{.data key="tracking.2026-09-19.country" d="0"}%]{.k .f}
[the same slice re-asked on 19 September 2026 to 21 models, 14 of them released after July]{.l}
:::
::: {.stat}
[43% · 15%]{.k .f}
[the shares among the 14 new models alone, whose averages sit between 39 and 55 percent]{.l}
:::
:::

::: {.prose}
[Exploratory, outside the pre-registration. Question 1, age 40, Version B in the six English-prompt countries and B-cross elsewhere, 25 answers per cell. [Back to the talk](#reveal).]{.source}
:::

::: {.notes}
The English slice is a conservative test for country effects: asking in the local language roughly doubles the country share. Among the new models Brazil gets 38 percent and Turkey 51, and Turkey, where the unhedged benchmark is lowest, ranks near the top.

Four of the seven carried-over models give the same average within half a point. DeepSeek V4 Flash moved 8.5 points under an unchanged identifier, the size of a country contrast, so replications should report the collection date.
:::

## Thirteen models are thirteen clusters {#room-inference visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.split .even .cols}
::: {.prose}
[Estimation]{.colhead}

The advice $y_{imc}$ of repetition $i$ by model $m$ for country $c$ is regressed on model fixed effects and country effects relative to the U.S.

Standard errors cluster on the model. With 13 clusters every p-value is a wild cluster bootstrap with Webb six-point weights and 9,999 replications.

The twenty country contrasts are one Holm family. The minimum detectable single contrast is about 4 points.
:::
::: {.prose}
[Collection]{.colhead}

Temperature 0.7, no system prompt, at most 4,000 tokens, truncated answers excluded.

A JSON-first parser recovered a number from 99.9% of answers. There were no refusals in 267,150 answers.

The joint test of equal advice in all 21 countries gives F(20, 12) = 20.56, p = 0.006.
:::
:::

[[Back to the countries](#countries) · [Back to the design](#design)]{.figcap}

::: {.notes}
Why the model is the unit: repetitions within a model are not independent, so the effective sample is the thirteen models, not the quarter-million answers. Asymptotic CR1 with G = 13 over-rejects badly, which is why the bootstrap is the inference of record.

The pilot of about 6,800 queries passed three pre-specified gates before filing: parse rate at least 95 percent per model, refusal ceilings, and between-model dispersion of the country contrast no larger than 0.06.
:::

## In the large-effect countries, most of the gap attaches to the country name {#room-decomp visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.notes}
Each bar stacks the three cues into the gap between the fully localized Version C and the U.S. English generic prompt. In the large-effect countries, Brazil, Italy, Poland, Mexico, the dark country-name slab carries most of it. The country-name slab also changes the currency and the numeral of the amount, which move with the country reference.

Japan is the clearest exception: a positive language slab of about four points. The dollar-stake room checks whether the yen numeral drives it.

::: {.notes}
Temperature only affects dispersion, and mildly: the mean within-cell standard deviation rises from 0.035 at temperature 0 to 0.041 at 1.0. Numeral anchoring cannot manufacture Brazil's eleven points: Japan's contrast is +1.2 with native numerals and an implied −1.6 with the dollar statement, small either way.

Replacing the thirteen model fixed effects with six vendor fixed effects leaves every contrast essentially unchanged, though six clusters support no formal inference.
:::

## A separate model codes every explanation, and pension and horizon appear in nearly all of them {#room-coding visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.stats}
::: {.stat}
[[ ]{.data key="textCats.horiz.B" pct="0"}%]{.k .f}
[of explanations mention the horizon]{.l}
:::
::: {.stat}
[[ ]{.data key="textCats.pens.B" pct="0"}%]{.k .f}
[mention an existing pension]{.l}
:::
::: {.stat}
[[ ]{.data key="textCats.local.B" pct="0"}%]{.k .f}
[name local financial context]{.l}
:::
:::

::: {.prose}
One model outside the panel, Claude Opus 4.7, codes each explanation, shown only its text and not the country, the model or the allocation. A panel of four judges from other vendor families validated the codes before any coefficient was estimated, with minimum pairwise Cohen's κ of 0.95 for inflation, 0.95 for pension and 0.87 for local context.

[Version B, Question 1, age 40, all 21 countries. [Back to the talk](#words).]{.source}
:::

::: {.notes}
The horizon category is in every explanation, so it has no country variation to test. Pension and horizon are both named in essentially every answer, and only horizon moves the number: how often a consideration is mentioned says nothing about whether it is used.

Inflation reasoning is elevated exactly in the high-inflation economies: +56 points in Turkey and +33 in South Africa against a U.S. base of 34 percent. A multilingual keyword dictionary agrees with the judge on 99, 96 and 73 percent of rows.
:::

## On the mortgage, advice sits 13 to 36 points above the benchmark in every calibration country {#room-mortbench visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.split .wide-left .center-v}
```{=html}
<div class="stage" data-chart="mortbench"></div>
```

::: {.prose}
Prepaying a mortgage earns the after-tax real mortgage rate for sure, so the benchmark is the Merton share with that rate as the safe return.

Advice exceeds it in all 16 calibration countries, by 13 to 36 points. Emily's gap is the largest: theory [ ]{.data key="c.USA.q2alpha" pct="0"}%, advice [ ]{.data key="c.USA.q2mean" pct="0"}%. The slope of advice on theory, 0.24, is not distinguishable from zero.

[Exploratory, not in the pre-registration. [Back to the talk](#mortgage).]{.source}
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Japan has the lowest benchmark, 20 percent, because its after-tax real mortgage rate is the highest, and it gets the lowest advice, 54 percent. Among the nine non-U.S. countries with benchmarks below 0.40 the gap stays between 29 and 34 points, so the advice rises with the benchmark almost point for point there.

The calibration slope is 0.24 on the mortgage question against 0.07 on the portfolio question for the same fifteen countries. With fifteen countries neither is distinguishable from zero, and both intervals exclude one.
:::

## In Brazil, Turkey and Mexico the inflation answer switches to inflation-linked bonds {#room-inflation visibility="uncounted"}

```{=html}
<div class="stage tall" data-chart="inflation"></div>
```

[[Back to the talk](#mortgage)]{.figcap}

::: {.notes}
Equities are the primary instrument in 93 percent or more of answers in fourteen countries. Brazil: 87 percent inflation-linked bonds. Turkey: 66 percent linkers and 16 percent gold. Mexico 58 percent linkers, Poland split. Even inside the English-prompting group, India and South Africa tilt toward protection, against under 3 percent in the U.S., UK, Canada and Australia.

There were no refusals on this question, although several models noted the 1 percent rate was unrealistically low, most often for Turkey.
:::

## The country effects are only weakly related to national risk preferences and literacy {#room-prefs visibility="uncounted"}

```{=html}
<div class="stage" data-chart="prefs"></div>
```

[[Back to the talk](#bench)]{.figcap}

::: {.notes}
A country one standard deviation more risk-tolerant gets under three points more equity, and the widest preference contrast in the panel, Japan to South Africa, predicts under four. South Africa, by far the most risk-tolerant, gets slightly less than the U.S.

This is descriptive: the prompt describes one investor, not a country mean, and imputing national risk-taking to her is an ecological inference an advisor need not make. Leave-one-out slopes stay positive and small. The two-stage bootstrap intervals exclude zero, and the wild bootstrap over countries does not.
:::

## The benchmark: the Merton share for the stake, and a corner once the balance sheet counts {#room-benchmark visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.split .even .cols}
::: {.prose}
[Benchmark S: the stake alone]{.colhead}

$\theta^{*}_c = \dfrac{\mu_c - r_c}{\gamma\,\sigma_c^{2}}$ at $\gamma = 3$. The equity premium is common across currencies by uncovered interest parity, so only $\sigma_c$ differs.

Unhedged, theory spans [ ]{.data key="stats.alphaSMin" d="2"} (Turkey) to [ ]{.data key="stats.alphaSMax" d="2"} (South Korea). The calibration slope is [ ]{.data key="stats.kappa" d="2"}. Dropping Brazil lowers it to 0.03, dropping Turkey raises it to 0.21.
:::
::: {.prose}
[Benchmark I: the whole balance sheet]{.colhead}

Pension wealth and human capital enter as safe outside wealth $B$, scaling the demand of the liquid stake $L$ to $\theta^{*}(1 + B/L)$.

For a \$50,000 stake that is at the 100% corner in every country, far above any answer in the data.

Inverting the Merton rule, the advice implies relative risk aversion near 2 for stated-tolerant, 5 for stated-averse and 3 for no statement.
:::
:::

[Appendix B of the paper. [Back to the talk](#bench).]{.source}

::: {.notes}
The influence diagnostics are why the unhedged slope should not be over-read: it rests on the two most volatile currencies. Every other leave-one-out slope is between 0.11 and 0.15.

Omissions and their direction: static model (mean reversion would justify more equity for the young), labor income risk as a single loading, no taxes on returns, an average earner in every country, and local government bonds treated as riskless in real terms.
:::

## Each stated-investor cell adds one institution-free sentence to the English prompt {#room-wording visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.split .even .cols}
::: {.prose}
[Risk tolerance and pension, fully crossed]{.colhead}

*Tolerant:* "I am comfortable with substantial fluctuations in my portfolio value, including potential short-term losses, if it means higher expected returns over time."

*Generous pension:* "I will receive a substantial pension when I retire, projected to replace most of my pre-retirement income."

The mirror sentences state discomfort with fluctuations and a small pension.
:::
::: {.prose}
[Mean recommended share in each cell]{.colhead}

| | limited pension | generous pension |
|---|---|---|
| risk-averse | [ ]{.data key="stated.cells.averseLimited" d="2"} | [ ]{.data key="stated.cells.averseGenerous" d="2"} |
| risk-tolerant | [ ]{.data key="stated.cells.tolerantLimited" d="2"} | [ ]{.data key="stated.cells.tolerantGenerous" d="2"} |

*Horizon:* "over a five-year horizon" becomes one year ([ ]{.data key="stated.cells.h1" d="2"}) or twenty years ([ ]{.data key="stated.cells.h20" d="2"}), with no other change.
:::
:::

[English Question 1, age 40, all 21 countries with their local amounts, about 13,600 answers per cell. [Back to the talk](#levers).]{.source}

::: {.notes}
The statements are length-matched and institution-free, so acting on them needs no knowledge of local pension systems. That sharpens the compression result: a calibration slope near zero could reflect ignorance of local pensions, but the models also fail to use pension generosity when it is handed to them.

Two of thirteen models are nearly horizon-invariant, while the most responsive moves 79 points between one year and twenty. The risk-tolerance response is positive for all thirteen models and within a 3-point band across the 21 countries.
:::
